text: Picture this: you present a model's accuracy on Monday. On Thursday your manager reruns your notebook and gets a slightly different number. Or a teammate clones your project and it crashes on their laptop. Neither of you did anything wrong on purpose — the analysis simply wasn't reproducible. It depended on randomness, library versions, file locations, or data that nobody wrote down.

Computers generate pseudo-random numbers from a starting value called a seed — same seed, same sequence. NumPy's recommended approach creates a generator with an explicit seed: np.random.default_rng(42). Two generators built with seed 42 agree exactly every time, while two unseeded generators almost never do. The number 42 has no special meaning — pick any integer and keep it.

Randomness also hides inside pandas and scikit-learn, and they take a random_state argument. df.sample with random_state=42 on a ten-row table returns order IDs 9, 2, and 6 every single time, and train_test_split's test set is the same rows on every run. Get in the habit of setting random_state everywhere you split, sample, shuffle, or train a model that uses randomness.

The same code can behave differently across library versions, so record exactly what you used. Create a virtual environment for each project with python dash m venv dot venv, then capture what's installed with pip freeze redirected into requirements dot t x t. A teammate recreates that exact environment with pip install dash r requirements dot t x t. Commit that file next to your code, and note your Python version too.

pd.read_csv with a path like C colon slash Users slash alex slash Desktop works on exactly one computer. Build paths relative to the script instead: Path of underscore underscore file underscore underscore, dot resolve, dot parent locates the script itself, so the project works wherever it's cloned. In a notebook, underscore underscore file underscore underscore doesn't exist — use paths relative to the project folder instead.

hashlib.sha256 on the raw file's bytes produces a 64-character fingerprint of its exact contents. If the data changes by even one character, the fingerprint changes completely. Print it or save it alongside your results, and you can prove which data version produced them. Also treat raw data as read-only — cleaning code should read from data slash raw and write to a different place, never overwrite the original.

A short checklist: seed every random step and record the seed, pin versions in requirements dot t x t, use relative paths built with pathlib, keep raw data untouched and fingerprint it, and restart and run everything from scratch before you share.

To recap: seeds make randomness repeatable, pinned requirements make environments repeatable, relative paths make projects portable, and fingerprints make data traceable. With these, your Thursday number matches your Monday number. Next comes the Capstone, where we use everything in this course on one dataset, end to end.
